title: Chickenpox contact in pregnancy (telephone) — prioritise the dangerous decision

blocks.text: Chickenpox contact in pregnancy (telephone) — prioritise the dangerous decision

AMaC MRCP PACES23 • Round 5 • R5-230 • Station 2: Consultation (acute presentation) • 20 minutes • Skills A–G (clinical examination as indicated) • 14 October 2026 • Unofficial educational marking descriptors

You are taking a telephone call from a woman at 22 weeks of pregnancy whose child developed chickenpox yesterday. She cannot recall having chickenpox and asks if her baby is safe. Take a focused history, assess immediate safety and agree the initial management with the patient or caller.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: HOOK: A potentially susceptible pregnant woman with significant VZV exposure; susceptibility must be checked rather than assumed.

TRAP: Advise immediate assessment for chickenpox symptoms, especially fever with breathlessness, severe rash or neurological symptoms. Avoid contact with other susceptible pregnant women and neonates if infectious; explain follow-up without falsely guaranteeing fetal safety.

rows: “I need to check whether you need urgent help.”

Advise immediate assessment for chickenpox symptoms, especially fever with breathlessness, severe rash or neurological symptoms. Avoid contact with other susceptible pregnant women and neonates if infectious; explain follow-up without falsely guaranteeing fetal safety.
“I’ll ask questions that distinguish the causes.”
Ask when the rash began, whether the household exposure is ongoing, past chickenpox or two vaccine doses, gestation, any current rash or fever, immune suppression and reliable contact details.
“There is a concern that needs checking.”
A potentially susceptible pregnant woman with significant VZV exposure; susceptibility must be checked rather than assumed.
Arrange urgent VZV IgG if history is uncertain and no evidence of immunity; contact obstetrics/virology and use the current UKHSA PEP pathway.

“The first decision is whether the patient needs emergency assessment now.”

“Before assuming that diagnosis, I should consider: Immunity from previous disease or vaccination changes the need for prophylaxis. A current chickenpox rash changes the pathway from exposure prophylaxis to treatment.”

Avoid contact with other susceptible pregnant women and neonates if infectious; explain follow-up without falsely guaranteeing fetal safety.”

Immunity — Elicits reliable previous infection/vaccination history and arranges VZV antibody testing if unclear. Escalates promptly for time-dependent management based on verified immune status
Assessment — Asks about maternal fever, rash or respiratory symptoms and gestation. Differentiates asymptomatic exposure from established infection requiring urgent care

Prophylaxis — Uses current UKHSA pathway for susceptible exposed pregnant women, including oral antiviral post-exposure prophylaxis when eligible. Checks contraindications, renal function and specialist advice; avoids outdated routine VZIG advice

Timing — Explains antiviral prophylaxis is generally started day 7 after exposure and continued to day 14 under applicable guidance: aciclovir 800 mg four times daily, or valaciclovir 1 g three times daily, for 7 days (UKHSA v9.0, March 2026). Documents exposure timing and provides an explicit follow-up and prescribing pathway

THINK: A potentially susceptible pregnant woman with significant VZV exposure; susceptibility must be checked rather than assumed. SAY: explain uncertainty clearly. DO: Arrange urgent VZV IgG if history is uncertain and no evidence of immunity; contact obstetrics/virology and use the current UKHSA PEP pathway. NUMBERS: 20-minute consultation. TRAP: Advise immediate assessment for chickenpox symptoms, especially fever with breathlessness, severe rash or neurological symptoms. Avoid contact with other susceptible pregnant women and neonates if infectious; explain follow-up without falsely guaranteeing fetal safety. FINISH: For significant exposure in a non-immune pregnant woman, oral aciclovir or valaciclovir is first-line PEP, starting on day 7 after exposure and continuing to day 14 according to the 2024 RCOG update and current UKHSA guidance. Immunoglobulin is an alternative only where antivirals cannot be used, guided by specialists.
